values.value: Why MCP Is Awesome: A New Contract Between AI and Your Tools
The Model Context Protocol turns "the AI guessed an API" into "the AI called a documented tool." Here's why that shift matters.

value.markup: Every AI assistant eventually hits the same wall: it's great at reasoning, mediocre at knowing which button to press. For years, the answer was bespoke integrations — one plugin per app, one schema per vendor, glued together with hope. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) replaces that patchwork with a single, open contract: any client that speaks MCP can discover and call tools from any server that implements it, without either side knowing the other exists in advance.

values.value: A shared protocol means fewer one-off wires between systems.

value.markup:
What makes this genuinely exciting isn't the transport — JSON-RPC over stdio or HTTP is unglamorous by design. It's the discovery. A server exposes its tools, resources and prompts with real schemas, and a client can list them at runtime. That means an assistant working inside Umbraco.Bench can ask "what can I do here?" and get back a live answer: create a document type, move a data type, publish a page — the exact vocabulary this project's own MCP server exposes, no bespoke glue code required on either side.

It also means the boundary between "the model" and "the system" gets a lot cleaner. Instead of an LLM improvising a raw HTTP call against an API it half-remembers, it calls a named tool with a validated payload, and gets back a structured result it can reason about. Errors are typed. Side effects are explicit. Nobody has to trust the model to have memorized your OpenAPI spec correctly.

values.value: MCP is the difference between an assistant that guesses your API and one that reads your menu.

value.markup: None of this required us to write a single migration or hand-roll a content API for this blog. Every document type, data type, block, and piece of content on this page was created by an agent talking to Umbraco's own MCP server — the same server you'd point any other MCP-aware client at. That's the real pitch: not a smarter model, but a common language that lets any sufficiently capable model operate your tools safely.

values.value: 5 Reasons MCP Changes How We Build With AI
From live schema discovery to zero-glue integrations, here are five concrete reasons the Model Context Protocol earns the hype.

value.markup: MCP has been out long enough to stop being a novelty and start being infrastructure. Here are five reasons it's earned a permanent spot in how we build AI-assisted tools — drawn straight from building this very blog with it.

1. One protocol, any tool

A single MCP client can talk to a filesystem server, a database server, and a CMS server like Umbraco's without custom adapters for each. The client learns capabilities at runtime instead of baking in assumptions at build time.

2. Schemas the model can actually read

Every tool ships a JSON schema for its inputs. That turns "hope the model formats this right" into "validate before you call it" — the difference between a flaky demo and something you'd run unattended.

values.value: Structured tool calls, not scraped screenshots.

value.markup:
3. Local-first by default

The reference transports are stdio and local HTTP. Your data doesn't need to leave the machine for the model to act on it — the Umbraco MCP server used to build this site never left localhost.

4. Composable agents

Because servers are interchangeable, an agent's capability set is just "which servers are attached today." Add a server, gain a skill — no redeploying the assistant.

5. It documents itself

Tool descriptions double as onboarding docs for both humans and models. Reading this project's MCP configuration and tool list tells you almost everything about what the assistant is allowed to touch.

values.value: The best integrations are the ones you don't have to write twice.
Every engineer who has maintained two SDKs for the same API

value.markup: This entire blog — document types, blocks, media, and the two posts you're reading — was modeled and published through the Umbraco MCP server, live, without a single migration file. That's not a party trick; it's what happens when the protocol does its job.
